speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport); Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: that Bill C-93, an act to amend the Bretton Woods and Related Agreements Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, it is surprising that Bill C-93 is not being spoken to by a member of the government to introduce to the House and to the people watching us the importance of this piece of legislation.
It is a bill which brings into effect certain amendments made to an international agreement to which Canada is a party, establishing the International Monetary Fund. The effect of the legislation and of that agreement entered into earlier this year by members of the International Monetary Fund is to increase Canada's quota, as well as the quota of many other nations, to the fund and to provide certain additional sanctions for borrowers from the International Monetary Fund who failed to meet their obligations.
I am sure that all members of the House are well aware of the success of the International Monetary Fund, as an international institution, in providing a means of funding the balance of payments of nations around the world. It has been a useful institution in providing advice and direction to many countries, both
developing countries as well as developed countries, in the context of providing the financial services that it does.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance); Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank our colleagues on the other side of the House. I guess it is because of my inexperience that I was bobbing up and down here, two or three times. I am not just sure exactly when you have to have your head up and when you have to have your head down. I can assure the hon. Whip of the Liberal Party that I also have taken an oath of office and I will try to fulfil my responsibilities to the best of my ability.
I would like to begin today's debate on Bill C-93, proposing amendments to the Bretton Woods and Related Agreements Act, by reminding members of the International Monetary Fund's role in the world financial system. The International Monetary Fund, or IMF, is a central institution of the international monetary system.
The IMF has two central roles. First, it monitors the economic policies of all its member countries, assessing the consistency of policies among countries and providing policy advice. Second, it provides credit to countries facing balance of payments financing problems. For the most part, financing is provided on the condition that countries undertake policy reforms designed to eliminate the imbalances within their economies, thus creating the conditions necessary for sustainable, non-inflationary growth.
The IMF's continuing ability to operate effectively is crucial to the smooth operation of the world monetary and financial system. This is particularly the case in the early 1990s, when the international financial situation is facing difficult and challenging conditions. There is uncertainty about the world economic outlook and prospects for further sustained global economic growth arising from a number of factors. Foremost among these is the crisis in the Persian Gulf. The evolution of global payments imbalances necessitates a continuing need for balance of payments financing, possibly on a substantial scale.
An agreement was reached last spring by the fund's interim committee-the major policy advisory body of the Fund which, to our honour, is chaired by the hon. Minister of Finance-to increase total fund capital subscriptions by 50 per cent. Quotas are an important feature of the IMF. They serve three purposes in its operations.
First, the quotas which members subscribe are the major source of funds which the IMF lends to countries in balance of payments difficulties in order to correct their imbalances, without resorting to protectionist or other disruptive measures.
Second, quotas serve to determine the amounts which members can borrow under the various facilities of the IMF. Finally, quotas determine the voting strength of members and the composition of the executive board.
The proposed increase in IMF quotas is part of a regular cycle for reviewing fund quotas. The higher level of total IMF quotas is required to ensure a better balance between the resources available to the IMF, and the needs of members for balance of payments financing over the next few years.
While other institutions will provide the bulk of development financing for the developing world, the IMF has the specific responsibility to use its resources in support of growth-oriented economic adjustment programs, for both developing and developed countries. In turn, IMF financing should catalyze additional financing from private and official sources.
There will be a need for the fund to continue to play a major role in the international debt strategy by supporting countries which are having problems servicing their external debts in their efforts to restore creditworthiness. Developing countries have made extensive use of IMF funding in recent years, and will likely continue to do so.
For its part, the fund has shown innovation and flexibility in its policies in response to the special needs of the major debtor countries. One clear example of that innovation was the decision to use IMF resources and those of the World Bank to permit developing countries to buy back a portion of their commercial debt at a discount in the secondary market, thus reducing their over-all debt burden. The proposed increase in IMF quotas would create scope for similar innovation in response to future needs.
December 7, 1990

But fund resources are not restricted simply to the developing countries. An important element of the fund's activities in the period ahead will be to facilitate market oriented reforms in east European countries. In fact, the emerging democracies of eastern Europe are already looking to the IMF for advice and financial support. Poland, Hungary and Yugoslavia currently have fund programs, including policy guidance as well as financial support. Czechoslovakia and Bulgaria have recently joined the fund and have already begun policy discussions with the IMF staff. We expect close co-operation among the IMF, the World Bank, and the new European Bank for Reconstruction and Development in support of the economic transformation that is now taking place and will be required in eastern Europe.
The last increase in fund quotas was seven years ago. That increase served to support in conjunction with large-scale borrowing the fund's policies on the use of its resources in responding to the debt problems of many developing countries. During that period, however, arrears to the IMF accumulated and it started to threaten the fund's continued ability to assist members in dealing with their balance of payments problems. The reason for the accumulation of arrears by countries such as Sudan, Liberia, Peru and Vietnam are many and complex.
However, one characteristic is shared by all these countries. Each has suffered from a fundamental failure to deal with its economic problems head on through a commitment to sustained economic policy reform.
In response to its mounting arrears problem, the fund has undertaken policies to prevent arrears from increasing and to promote the elimination of existing arrears. As a further measure to strengthen the funds arrears strategy, it was agreed during the quota negotiations that the quota increase would be conditional upon the passage of an amendment to the articles of the agreement, allowing for suspension of the voting rights of members in arrears.
This would be an intermediate step between powers which the IMF already has under the articles. The articles it has now is an initial sanction of suspension of borrowing rights and the ultimate sanction of expulsion.
Government Orders
The new quotas will come into effect when members having 85 per cent of present quotas have consented to the increases in their quotas and to the suspension amendment.
I would also note for the House that at the Houston economic summit last July, the Prime Minister and the leaders of the other major industrial countries called on the IMF, the World Bank, the OECD and the New European Bank for Reconstruction and Development to conduct an extensive evaluation of the economic situation of the Soviet Union. This study is now progressing, reinforcing the vital and central role of the IMF in the entire world economy.
The fund must also stand ready to deal with crisis situations, both with regard to individual members as well as more systemic threats to the international monetary system. The fund has recently demonstrated its flexibility in responding to countries affected by the events in the Middle East and will be a key player in helping these countries adjust to changed economic circumstances.
It is in this context, Mr. Speaker, that I propose the legislation before us today, Bill C-93, to amend the Bretton Woods and Related Agreements Act. Bill C-93 is a central element in Canada's continuing commitment to the smooth functioning of the international monetary system. It provides for an increase in Canada's quota subscription in the International Monetary Fund from 2,941 million special drawing rights, or SDRS, to 4,320.3 million SDRS.
This is confusing, Mr. Speaker, to most people in the House and I am sure to most people following. In Canadian dollars this would mean an increase in Canada's quota from approximately $4.9 billion to $7.2 billion, an increase of $2.3 billion.
I would note here, Mr. Speaker, that although our subscription in terms of Canadian dollars will increase by $2.3 billion, the actual Canadian dollar payment is $5.8 million.
This payment is a non-budgetary expenditure. Of the remainder, 25 per cent will be paid in special drawing rights from our international reserves, while the balance of our commitment is held in reserve in the event that the IMF needs to draw upon additional resources. Commensurately, the larger IMF quota adds to the

December 7, 1990
Government Orders
resources available to Canada in the event of balance of payments needs.
The increase in Canada's quota will allow us to continue to lead a constituency at the fund, composed of Ireland and a number of Caribbean countries.
More important, agreement by Parliament to the proposed amendments to the IMF articles will allow Canada to maintain an effective voice on the IMF issues.
Canada has been a full participant in the activities of the IMF and strongly supports its role as a central institution in the international monetary system. In order for the IMF to continue to play a critical and an effective role in the system, and in order to Canada to show leadership on international financial matters, Canada must act to ratify the quota increase and suspension amendment.
Recent developments in the Gulf and uncertainties in the world economy makes it desirable to bring the quota increase into effect at the earliest possible date. I believe strongly that it is important that Canada show leadership by earlier ratification of the amendment.
Our legislative approval of the quota increase and a suspension amendment will demonstrate the importance Canada attaches to the role of the fund.
I urge my hon. colleagues in the House to give timely consideration and early passage to this bill.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I would like to thank the parliamentary secretary for providing me with
a copy of his remarks. With respect to his comments concerning the IMF and Canada's role in it, I am pleased to associate myself with those remarks.
As I was saying earlier, the IMF has performed a very useful and distinguished role in the world economy. Canada has been an active participant in the activities of this fund since it was established after the Second World War. I believe we should continue to strongly support the IMF in its central position in international financial matters. Consequently, I do not see that there will be any difficulty in the Official Opposition supporting the proposed amendments to the agreement, as Canada has already agreed to these, because they make ultimate sense in the context of the international arrangements.
I would like, though, to draw out one point that the parliamentary secretary did refer to in his remarks. This would be of concern to many of our constituents. In increasing Canada's quota in the fund, there is no impact on the budgetary position of the Government of Canada.
Essentially, what we are being asked to do is to increase the amount of special drawing rights that are held on account in the International Monetary Fund for Canada. It is as though we are putting additional funds into a different bank account. It is not an expenditure. It does not affect our ability to pay for other things. I think it is important that Canadians understand that.
What we are doing here is agreeing to an increased commitment to international financial stability in not committing ourselves to an increased expenditure of Canadian taxpayers' money.
As I understand it, the actual amount of cash to move from Canada into the fund which would be on deposit for Canada is in the order of $6 million which, while a lot for an individual, is not a lot for the Government of Canada, nor is it an expenditure by the Government of Canada. The only thing I can say about this bill that gives me any cause for concern is the fact that the Minister of Finance for Canada played a role in negotiating these amendments to the agreement. That gives me cause to pause, given the condition of our economy at the present time. Despite that reservation that I expressed, I can say on behalf of the Official Opposition that we will be supporting this bill.
December 7, 1990

Mr. Speaker, I must say that I am slightly shocked that the member from the Liberal Party that will, without question, support this kind of a bill. We recognize the need for this and the need for it being in place.
His party and the party across the way were both signatories to a report which was established by the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade called Securing our Global Future which indicated very specific concern with the method that the World Bank and the IMF are following.
Although this bill has a very innocuous name, the Bretton Woods and Related Agreements Act, it is a very misleading title. Perhaps when these institutions were put in place in 1944 they had some specific value. They operated at that time to aid the world.
This act has done a lot to enslave much of the Third World. It was not intended to do this. Enslavement is not in the mandate of either the international bank for reconstruction and development, nor is it in the list of purposes for the International Monetary Fund. After all these years, enslavement has been the result for millions of people in countries which have taken the bait and thought that they were on their way to prosperity and health by borrowing from these august institutions.
In fact, most of the Third World countries which have accepted this process are harvesting death, hunger and increasing poverty. I am not suggesting that was the mandate, but that is the result. Canada has not helped to alleviate that result. We are being asked here today to acquiesce once more, without thought or without analysis, to being part of the failure of this world financial structure. Should Canada yield to the world financial institutions and put its signature to the disaster of unmanageable Third World debt? Should it stay part of this structure?
This debt is having the effect, as I said before, of killing children, starving people and devastating the countries which have accepted it. For what? It is designed to protect the financial system from its own failure. Failure is the only term that I can really apply to the impact of the Third World debt and the relationship of those Third World countries to the Bretton Woods institution.
Government Orders
On Thursday, June 7, 1990, the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade passed its fifth report entitled Securing our Global Future, Canada's stake in the unfinished business of Third World debt. That committee requested a comprehensive response in accordance with Standing Order 109 from the Government of Canada.
The report was an invitation to the Government of Canada to take some leadership in solving the problems of Third World debt. It was a plea from the members of the committee, members of every party in this House, to the Government of Canada to take some action to break the tradition of accepting the World Bank and IMF domination and say that people are more important than some myth which these financial institutions perpetrate, a myth that the world will fall apart if these debts are not paid back to the IMF or the World Bank, and if they are not paid on time and paid in full.
What this bill does is add to the quota and make more money available to Third World countries because they are in trouble as a result of having borrowed previously.
The committee recommended and specifically urged Canada to seek the support of other governments for an international conference on debt and sustainable global adjustment. Such a conference would aim for negotiated commitments to policy reform by all countries, not only the poor and indebted. One of the things that our international financial structure has done to these Third World countries is to enslave them by saying: "If you want money to pay your debt, you must follow certain requirements", and certain conditions are put in place.
The subsequent recommendation of this committee spelled out the principles and directions that it thought should be the basis of the process of global reform in handling Third World debt. Canada was asked by the committee to take a leadership role, and Canada came up lacking. The response to this report, which was required under the regulations, did not pick up any of the recommendations. Instead of a world conference which would look at world debt, it suggested a seminar. It denied the Third World countries a forum in which they could share the information as to how these institutions are affecting their economies. It refused to give these Third World countries an opportunity to share

December 7, 1990
Government Orders
information about the pain and distress that they are feeling. Canada denied them this opportunity.
What does this have to do with the bill? I quote the committee report:
The sub-committee does not offer a blueprint, a perestroika, in a Bretton Woods institution such as the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund and the General Agreement on Thrifts and Hade. But we are convinced of the need for structural adjustments here, not just in developing countries, and not on the basis of some utopian ideal, but as a pragmatic necessity for the future of the planet.
There is no alternative to concerted political action among the major developed-country governments. Canada is a respected member of that group and active in many international organizations. We have a seat on the United Nations Security Council. Finance Minister Michael Wilson now chairs the key policy-advisory committee of the IMF's executive board. It is time for Canada to use its international position and influence to maximum advantage.
That was part of the report of an all-party committee of this House, its recommendations and its discussion with the government.
What is this debt that we have been discussing? There is a $1.3 trillion debt which has been accumulated by the developing countries. Sixty-seven of these countries, roughly one-half of all the so-called Third World countries, are experiencing debt servicing difficulties. It means that their debt has become unmanageable relative to their economies. Their indebtedness has threatened their economic development and political stability.
In most debtor nations, real per capita income has eroded in absolute terms to the position where their standard of living is at 1960s levels. The World Bank, but particularly the IMF, have invested in scheduling this $1.3 trillion worth of debt. That is what this money that we are talking about here today is for. The $1,378 billion that Canada is expected to come up with is for rescheduling by the IMF. It is intended to allow these countries to reschedule their debt. If one already has no possibility of paying the debt that one has, what value is rescheduling? It is fairly obvious that no amount of rescheduling can possibly resolve the problem.
In most of the debtor countries, the total national debt exceeds the total national income by several times. Also, debt services, that is interest paid on the debt and other services, are more-and this is an average across the
board-for these countries than two-thirds of these debtor countries' export earnings. Export earnings are the only way they can get the money. If the services take up two-thirds of those export earnings and they need something to live on, what is left? Therefore, the payment capacity of most debtor countries is declining even as the IMF is rescheduling their debt.
Mr. Speaker, do you get the feeling that this bill might just be asking us to throw some good money after bad? If we continue to use the structure that is in place, as far as the World Bank and the IMF is concerned, that is the only thing that we can assume. This seems to be an almost bottomless pit under these circumstances, a bottomless pit which is soaking up whatever funding is served up and will continue to do so.
The IMF and the World Bank are both institutions which are considered business-like in their approach. But what they have done, as do all banks-at least I am told-is through initial loans and rescheduling loaned at least $4 for every dollar that these institutions have received from their donors. Canada, of course, is one of those donors.
They have loaned out $4 for every dollar they have received from the donor. If this thing suddenly collapsed, not only would they lose the donors' contribution, but they would have to go to those donors and find another $3. They do not think that would happen. So they go on perpetuating their structure and hoping that some day it will clear itself up. I am not at all sure that that will happen.
When the World Bank and the IMF cannot collect from an impoverished country with an unmanageable debt, they impose what these institutions call structural adjustment. The World Bank and the IMF, and possibly commercial banks because they work through the IMF, will decide how a nation generates its wealth from now on.
For instance, if a country needs yams to feed its people, but it can sell bananas, it grows bananas because it will be able to sell those bananas and get some money. The people will go hungry. The World Bank and the IMF decide how people will spend any wealth that they manage to produce.

The first thing a country must do is pay the interest on its debt, whether the people are hungry or not. Then a country is required to pay, if possible, some of the principle but it is not supposed to any of that wealth that it has created to increase the people's productivity, such as on health and on education.
The World Bank and the IMF will tell these countries how to invest any wealth that they might have. They invest only in more banana fields, not in something which might, in the long term, increase their productivity. What the IMF and the World Bank want is shortterm cash tomorrow. A country produces bananas and sells them. There is no investment that might increase the standard of living of the people of that particular country.
Debtor countries are not free to set monetary or fiscal policy. They are not free to set export or import quantities. They are not free to set social and health programs, or wage and price policies. In other words, the structural adjustment has enslaved this nation, not only enslaved it, but removed democracy; democracy being the ability of the people of a country to make its own decisions. So they have eliminated democracy to a certain extent.
The debtor nation has by this process of structural adjustment given up its sovereignty and exchanged it for, what? Prosperity? No. It changed it for economic slavery.
Adolfo Perez Esquivel made a very worth-while statement. Esquivel is a broadcaster and a journalist in Costa Rica. He is also an 1980 Nobel Peace Prize winner. He puts it this way.
It isn't possible to think about real democracy if the economy of a country is oriented only towards satisfying the demands of the international banks.
Perez Esquivel worries that debt not only diminishes democracy, it also requires repression. Policies designed to pay the debt hurt the people; the people protest-and then governments turn to police and military forces to keep the lid on. Even civilian rulers use repression-when the belt has to be tightened more than the waistline permits.
That article is called "Low Intensity Democracy" and I commend it to anybody who is interested in this.
The article goes on to talk about the drain from Latin America and it says:
-creditor nations drained an estimated $500-billion out of Latin America in the form of debt service, profits, royalties and capital
Government Orders
flight. That haemorrhage reduced living standards to the levels they were 12 years ago; in some countries, per capita income has gone back two or three decades past-
But more common is the spread of hunger and disease that kills a thousand children a day in Brazil alone. Will millions of abandoned street kids believe in a democracy that does not believe in them?
That is part of an article about Latin America by Bob Carty.
The choice seems to be democracy or economic enslavement. The NGOs across Canada, in the United States and some of the other NGOs of the world have a position paper which they call "Working Group on the World Bank". This group has actually attempted to work with the World Bank. It has been in place for 10 years but has not been particularly successful. Hopefully in the last couple of years it is making a little bit of headway because I think the World Bank and the IMF are recognizing their failure.
It commends the World Bank for doing certain things and I would recommend again that anyone who is interested in this particular area should take a look at the position paper of the NGO working group on the World Bank because it makes a number of recommendations. It comments on the structural adjustment. It comments on conditionality. It comments on the World Bank and IMF effect on the environment. It abhors the lack of participation by Third World countries and the people of Third Work countries. It also abhors the lack of information given by people who are most affected by the decisions made by the World Bank and the IMF. I could spend a long time on the recommendations of the NGOs.
Our external affairs committee unanimously, everyone from all parties in this House, gave our government an opportunity to take a leading role. As I said earlier, the committee did establish Canadian principles upon which it believed that our government could develop a world strategy which would deal with debt, not only with Canada's relation to the rest of the world or to Third World countries, but that it should take a leadership role within the the IMF and the World Bank in which we have a certain amount of commitment and into which we have put a certain amount of money. We should take this opportunity to develop some kind of world leadership and use it. I want to just briefly cover a little bit of the guiding principles which the committee said Canada should look at when it started dealing with Third World debt. The committee suggested that the Third World

December 7, 1990
debt must allow sustainable human development in the debtor countries. It suggested that the creditor countries reduce the debt service on old debt and not impose it on any new debt. It suggested that poverty and debt are the enemies of development and, if you want development, you must eliminate both poverty and debt. Adjustment can only be successful and should be supported as part of the holistic development approach in co-operation with the debtor country. In other words, it is suggesting that maybe we should pay some attention to the people who are the recipients and that they be part of the decision-making process.
I know, when you walk into a bank, you are told that you can have money under certain conditions, and if you do not like these conditions, no money. That is almost exactly the way these institutions are dealing with the Third World countries. It suggests also that social impacts of adjustment programs must be assessed. A country should not be so constrained that it cannot maintain its basic social programs. Support for debt relief and structural adjustment should be determined, case by case, but according to consistent criteria which reflect Canadian values. This means the values of the Canadian public, I hasten to say, not the values of Canadian banks and financial institutions. Those values are: the commitment of debtor countries to reform to benefit the poor and the vulnerable groups, respect international norms of human rights, encourage democratic traditions, and eliminate the linkage of economic recovery and the debt so that there can be some kind of sustainable development allowed. That is the approach that the all-party committee recommended to the Government of Canada. Again, I have to say that the government came up lacking. Our friends in the opposition supported this as well.
Instead, what is the government doing? The government is asking us to pass this Bretton Woods bill and accept the old, unsuccessful methods of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund. The government is asking us to allow the kinds of things that have been done, for at least the last 20 years, to continue to be done. The original Bretton Woods institutions were established in 1944, as part of the reconstruction of Europe after the war and did, at that time, a considerable amount of good. But they do not fit the present structure and they should not be the bodies responsible
for the "elimination", and that is the only word I can use, of Third World debt.
The World Bank and the International Monetary Fund have failed in their mandate. They have failed to do what their mandate insists they should do. These institutions have shown they were a failure as long ago as 20 years.

Yesterday, there was a job; today, there is not, compliments of Prime Minister Grinch just before Christmas. It is cold comfort to hear on the air the President of the CBC say that he is sorry.

Marguerite D'Youville is the first Canadian bom saint. She was bom in Varennes, Quebec in 1701 and founded the Sisters of Charity, the Grey Nuns. This order has contributed to the early development of our country by educating the young and by caring for the sick and the less fortunate.
Under the leadership of Father Lacombe and Bishop Vital Grandin, the Grey Nuns were responsible for the first school and orphanage, and the first seniors' home in St. Albert. These were followed by hospitals in the province of Alberta.
Today, I join with Canadians from coast to coast to pay tribute to the Grey Nuns and their founder, Marguerite D'Youville.

Mr. Speaker, today marks the 15th anniversary of the illegal Indonesian invasion of East Timor. Nearly one third of the population of East Timor have been killed or starved since this brutal invasion.
The UN General Assembly and the UN Security Council adopted resolutions demanding Indonesia's immediate withdrawal from East Timor. Indonesia continues to defy the United Nations.
Canada abstained from the UN General Assembly resolution and has voted against resolutions endorsing East Timor's right to self-determination and humanitarian assistance. Since 1980, Canada has voted against the withdrawal of Indonesian forces from East Timor. Canada, of course, has more than $1 billion invested in Indonesia, being the third-largest foreign investor.
Canada's failure to support East Timor contradicts the position Canada has taken against the invasion of Kuwait by Iraq.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, farmers from my province of Prince Edward Island are following the GATT talks with baited breath in concern over the future of our supply management system.

There are over 600 dairy, egg and poultry farmers in Prince Edward Island whose livelihoods may be significantly altered by the results of the GATT negotiations taking place in Brussels. Both the National Farmers' Union and the P.E.I. Federation of Agriculture have expressed concern about the possibility of our supply management system being significantly altered by these negotiations.
Canada's system of orderly marketing has created the most efficient producers in the world. Our system is not geared to create surplus and has not contributed to the current trade distortions in agriculture.
I call on the government to consider the interests of the dairy, poultry and egg farmers in its negotiations in Brussels and I ask it to maintain its position to strengthen Article XI.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: GENERAL AGREEMENT ON TARIFFS AND TRADE
GENERAL AGREEMENT ON TARIFFS AND TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the fate of our garment workers is now in the hands of GATT. The results of the GATT talks have left the future of the Multi-Fibre Arrangement in limbo. With the recession, high interest rates, loss of consumer confidence, free trade, Mexico, the GST, GATT and the Multi-Fibre Arrangement, Canada's garment industry has more than enough on its plate.
Mr. Speaker, Canada has about 2,500 clothing manufacturers. In Quebec, this means 63,000 direct jobs and
100,000	indirect jobs. The industry generates sales totalling $8.5 billion in this country. The rules of international trade in the garment industry are changing too fast and on too many fronts at once.
Mr. Speaker, if the Multi-Fibre Arrangement is ever abolished, we must have a fairly long period of transition to allow the industry to adapt at the same rate as the United States, our principal trading partner.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, appearing before the parliamentary commission on the constitutional future of Quebec which held a hearing in
Hull on Wednesday, December 5, several witnesses stressed the lack of communication or co-operation, if you prefer, between the Government of Quebec and the federal government in a number of important areas.
Here in the Outaouais, one of the most important dossiers is the completion of highway 50 from the Outaouais to Montreal. Perhaps I may remind the people in our area that the agreements signed with the federal government go back to 1972, in which year the section from Hull to Masson was completed.
When the Parti Quebecois came to power in 1976, no funds were allocated by the Government of Quebec to complete the highway. In 1985, once again the Government of Quebec refused to invest any more money in completing the highway in the Outaouais. We are now in 1990, and the differences are political rather than constitutional. The reason why highway 50 in the Outaouais area is not being completed is because of political differences between both levels of government. We urge the federal government and the Quebec government to agree on an item that is extremely important to economic development in the Outaouais.

In an article I read recently, Raymond Gameau, ex-Finance critic of the federal Liberal Party, said that the goods and services tax proposed by the federal government was probably the fairest and least harmful tax to be found in this day and age of global markets.
Mr. Gameau explained that the existing federal tax on manufactured products was a disaster for Canadian industry because it was exported along with the products themselves, which made Canadian companies less competitive.
Mr. Gameau said that this tax was fair to everyone and would certainly prevent tax evasion to a considerable degree. He said it was the only solution the government had to raise more money, especially among big consumers.
As for the attitude taken by the Liberal senators, Mr. Gameau said it was unconscionable and an incredible

example of political partisanship. Nobody in his right mind believes that people welcome new taxes.
Mr. Speaker, here is another federal Liberal who finally saw the light. Liberal senators, stop fooling around and pass the GST-hurry up!

Mr. Speaker, there is growing concern among railway workers and the general public about recent changes in rail safety policy, changes which are increasing the risk to the public and worker safety.
CP Rail is allowing unsafe or bad order freight cars to leave Winnipeg for further destinations, instead of being repaired in Winnipeg where and when the defective components are discovered.
VIA Rail has done away with visual inspections of its passenger trains in Winnipeg, meaning that there are no inspections between Toronto and Vancouver, in spite of the fact that since May 11 rail workers have detected 15 defects on VIA trains.
CN Rail is violating Uniform Code of Operating Rules No. 104 by instructing its conductors to leave rail switches in the open position, instead of returning them to the appropriate configuration following the train movement.
The 1989 Summary of Railway Accidents and Incidents prepared by the Transportation Safety Board shows an 11.9 per cent increase in derailments on the main line tracks of CN and CP. This report indicates that approximately 40 per cent of the train derailments that have occurred on the main track over the past five years have resulted from defects on the track itself. Do you remember all the section gangs, Mr. Speaker, that were eliminated? The report also made the observation that "derailments due to equipment failure increased significantly in 1989".
There's more to come, thanks to the negligence of this government.

Mr. Speaker, the employees of CBC have once again been dealt a harsh blow. The recent announcement of spending cuts of $100 million dollars means close to 1,200 Canadians are out of a job.
It is saddening that a national institution like the CBC has to struggle to survive. Perhaps the government does not realize that it is cutting out the very heart of Canada.
Canadians last year were hit by VIA Rail cutbacks and now the government is cutting off CBC. With no transportation and no communication, how does the government expect to keep the country together?
Next Thursday, at noon on Parliament Hill, my colleagues and I will be joining other Canadians in a rally in support of our national institutions. I call on Canadians all across Canada to rally in support of the CBC.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to pay tribute to the memory of Jean Duceppe who died last night in Montreal.
Mr. Duceppe was a great Quebecer. Of humble origins, he played all the great roles on the stage. On radio, he was well known for his energy, humour, warmth and passionate feeling. On television, he played in some of our most popular "teleromans". On the stage, he acted in some of our best "beaux dimanches" offerings, and he even founded a theatre group which bears his name and which, I imagine, will continue to exist as living testimony to his talent.
As a union organizer, a nationalist and a performing artist, Jean Duceppe made a tremendous contribution to the world of the performing arts in Quebec. He leaves us a rich and challenging cultural heritage. With Jean Duceppe, our cultural roots have blossomed.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday across Canada we remembered last year's horror in Montreal. We remembered with grief and outrage the unnecessary death of 14 women. We remembered the hate and violence that caused those tragic deaths.
We must also remember that the hate and sickness that led to those murders occur to varying degrees every day in the country. It is simply not enough to remember that one horrible day. We must act to ensure that such a tragedy never occurs again. We must work to eliminate the ongoing abuse of women that occurs daily in our society.
This is not just a women's issue. As men, we have a particular responsibility. It is our daughters, our sisters, our wives, our mothers, and our friends who are at risk. For their sakes, and for those who are yet unborn, we must work together to guarantee them safe and secure futures.
The government must proceed as a minimum with tighter gun control legislation.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to join the Minister responsible for the Status of Women in marking the 20th anniversary of the release of the Royal Commission's Report on the Status of Women.
I would like to commend the efforts of the many groups and individuals who, over the past 20 years, have helped bring Canada to the level of equality we know today.
Women's groups across Canada were instrumental in the establishment of the royal commission and in providing input to it. They continue to be important agents for change in our country.
Following on the recommendations of the commission, women's directorates in all provinces and territories have been working hard over the years to improve the situation for women in their jurisdictions. Status of Women Canada has helped bring about change since
1976 by advising the minister and other federal departments and agencies on a wide range of issues affecting women. The Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women has also played a critical role in identifying and publicizing issues of concern to women since its establishment in 1973.
Let us recognize the collaborative efforts of these organizations.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today with regret to call attention to the continued problem of family violence that unfortunately characterizes our society.
On the same day that Canada and the House of Commons was commemorating 14 victims of violence in Montreal, we learned that a judge in Quebec City gave a man a suspended sentence for killing his wife. The judge commented on the wife's aggressiveness and vindictive personality as a cause. I regret, and I am certain this House regrets that once again a woman victim has been blamed for an act of violence that resulted in her death.
Those of us who have worked in social services and family court realize that domestic violence is rarely started by women. Yet, they are almost always the casualties of physical violence.
Yesterday, we showed our collective grief in commemorating 14 victims. Today, we must start dealing with violence, whenever we find it and wherever we find it, as a social problem to be attacked and eradicated.

subtopic: CANADIAN CHARTER OF RIGHTS AND FREEDOMS
CANADIAN CHARTER OF RIGHTS AND FREEDOMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Supreme Court ruled that the violation against the charter is justified in a free and democratic society. We either respect the charter or we do not.
Recently, on the basis of the charter, the justice system has protected the rights of women to have access to abortion, the rights of religious groups to wear turbans and carry kirpans, and the rights of refugees to have lengthy hearings. But when it comes to senior citizens who have contributed the most to the building of this

country, all of a sudden the justice system has double standards.
The justices of the Supreme Court have made a political decision and should be censured. I hope this House, which is the highest court of the land, will bring forward a motion showing the will of its members that this decision is unacceptable.

Mr. Speaker, a very sad news for Quebec this morning, the loss of Jean Duceppe, an outstanding artist who made his mark in Quebec history, a man who never left anyone indifferent. I felt a pang of anguish when I heard the sad news this morning. To me, Jean Duceppe was an artisan of Quebec proudness, for he made an exceptional contribution and used his remarquable talent to promote our culture. His heart-felt dedication, his love for Quebec will be our full inheritance. Wherever he is now I am sure he knows he can rely on his son Gilles, our colleague the hon. member for Laurier-Sainte-Marie, to uphold the legitimate aspirations of Quebec here in this House.
To his wife, to Gilles, to his children and grandchildren, to all the artists who will continue his work in Quebec, may I say on behalf of all Quebecers: Thank you, Jean, thank you for everything!

He stands up and asks what policies we are bringing forward. That is one. Another is the GST. If the hon. member will shake up his friends across the hall in the red Chamber and tell them to get on with taking a final vote on the GST, businesses which are planning for it will proceed with that and we can restructure our tax programs to help companies and businesses in this country, not hinder them, and create economic activity and employment. We have introduced the policies. The Grits in the Senate are holding it up.

Mr. Speaker, if there was any mystery about why this government is at

14 per cent in the polls it has got to be answered when the question "What will the government do to help Canadians?" is answered by "We'll bring in the GST". Who is going to believe that?
The monetary policy that this government has pursued so far has resulted in two things, the high unemployment rate that we see today and the government's budgetary deficit going further out of control so that it needs to borrow another $2.5 billion.
I ask the Prime Minister how the government can justify a monetary policy that one and the same time increases unemployment and increases the deficit?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member knows, we were left with a $200 billion debt and any additions to the debt today are compounded interest from the debt that was left when we took office in 1984. That is fact number one.
Second, the hon. member knows full well that the inflationary pressures in this country were at alarming proportions. They talk about the senior citizens and the low-income people. They are the ones who are hurt most by high inflation. When the Grits ignored high inflation, it went up to 13 per cent and 14 per cent, and who hurt the most? The unemployed, the poor in our economy, those on fixed incomes, and senior citizens.
This government was determined not to let that happen. Inflationary pressures are dropping. Interest rates are dropping. We want to get them down on a permanent basis. That is what this is all about for the economy of this country and its future.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the right hon. the Prime Minister. We are aware this morning that the unemployment rate has jumped again. The recession now has taken root nationwide in pretty well all regions of this country, with tremendous increases in unemployment. I would like to ask the Prime Minister, since we have in this country a made in Canada recession that was deliberately and methodically created by the Government of Canada to fight inflation by increasing interest rates and increasing the value of the Canadian dollar, what is the plan to fight the recession? What is the plan to put people back to work? We, in this party, have suggested a five-point
Oral Questions
program. What has he, as Prime Minister of Canada, going to do?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the New Democratic Party proposed a five-point program in a press release. There was no back-up material and no costing. Every single legitimate economist who has taken a look at it laughed, and said it would put this country into a recession like they have never seen before, causing very high interest rates and high inflation. Every economist has said that that is what would happen if the NDP brought in its policies. We do not plan to do that.

Mr. Speaker, it is about time the Prime Minister fired this minister. We call for a reduction, not an increase in interest rates.
As the leader of this country, I want to know from the Prime Minister of Canada whether in the last five or six months he has been to the unemployment lines that are getting longer and longer? Has he been to see the unemployed? Has he been to food banks in this country? Has he seen some of the almost million kids who are in poverty in Canada? What is going to say to all those people? Will he go down to those lines and talk to those poor people instead of spending all of his time sipping champagne, eating caviar, with his wealthy friends on Bay Street in Toronto?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the last time that I sipped champagne and had caviar was at a Socialist International convention, and I was an observer.
I share the sincere concern of my hon. friend about any increase in unemployment rates. I think he would acknowledge that when this government was sworn in, unemployment was at 11.6 per cent. It is now down to 9.1 per cent. In almost all of the provinces of Canada, including his own, unemployment has decreased very substantially over the period of time and employment has increased very dramatically.
For example, in the case of youth unemployment, which is a particular concern, it is down over 4 percentage points over the period of economic growth. It could not be otherwise because in the last six years, 1.5 million new jobs have been created in Canada, 83 per cent of them have been full time and 64 per cent of them have

December 7, 1990
Oral Questions
gone to women. During this period of time, Canada has led all of the OECD countries in terms of job creation. It is a very impressive job creation record.
We are going through a period, along with others, of economic difficulties. We recognize that. We are seeking to bring about lower interest rates to re-energize the economy to make sure that we go through another sustained period of impressive economic growth. We cannot do it artificially. We cannot do it by repealing the laws of economics and instructing anybody, tomorrow morning, to lower interest rates by 3.5 per cent. We must reduce the deficit, obtain the confidence of the international investment community, attract those investment funds and create the employment. That is the way the economy moves and that is what we are trying to do.

Mr. Speaker, as the Prime Minister is aware, the situation is worse now than it was last year. Canada is now in a full-scale recession. In Quebec, the unemployment rate has now reached 11.4 per cent.
What is the Prime Minister going to do now to create-and this is very important, Mr. Speaker-to create jobs for the unemployed in Baie Comeau and for welfare recipients in Montreal? What is he going to do now for people in Canada who are living in poverty? This is a question many thousands of Canadian men and women across this country are forced to ask. What is he going to do now? Figures are not enough. What kind of concrete action is he going to take for the benefit of those Canadians who are now living in poverty?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend is perfectly right. Figures as such don't mean a thing when we are talking about an individual or a family. That is why the economic progress we have experienced for six years is particularly encouraging. The nature of this progression is such that today,
956.000	Canadians are no longer living in poverty;
333.000	women and 297,000 children and 83,000 senior citizens are no longer living in poverty.
So I think that, although our programs still leave much to be desired, we have made progress towards a fairer and more equitable deal for Canadians. Job creation and the resulting prosperity have been relatively equally
distributed throughout our society. These figures are still quite substantial. Nearly one million Canadians more managed to get out of the poverty cycle during the past six years, including children, the elderly and families.
Last Saturday, some new figures came out, which indicate:

"Average family income in Canada now exceeds $50,000 for the first time in our history." This is the kind of sustained economic growth that we have been working on, and I think my hon. friend would agree with me that, while we have difficulties, there are areas of substantial encouragement.

Mr. Speaker, I don't think the Prime Minister should brag about these figures, because they show that in the past year, nearly 24 per cent of our jobs were lost-232,000 Canadians less are working this year compared with last year, in other words, 1,217,000 Canadians and their families will not be able to afford Christmas because they are out of work. I therefore want to ask the Prime Minister and his government exactly what kind of policy they have that will give hope to these millions of Canadians and their families who can't even think about buying Christmas presents for their children.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we want to ensure that programs are aligned with dropping interest rates. We now see the beneficial effects of these reductions, which although they are relatively modest, are being sustained and are starting to have a beneficial impact on the economy. Once this impact has been absorbed by the economy, we will see a drop in the deficit, and we will experience sustained economic recovery. What we see this morning is what we are seeing in the United States and in many countries throughout the world.
I agree with my hon. friend that figures as such don't mean a lot, and with the hon. member I also deplore the existence of these very human problems in a society like ours. However, as I just mentioned to my NDP friend from Saskatchewan, today, nearly one million Canadians less are living in poverty, thanks to the economic growth we experienced in Canada during the past six years. And

She said: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to begin third reading debate on this bill.
This bill was introduced to implement the Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods which was adopted in Vienna in 1980 under the auspices of the United Nations so as to allow federal entities to benefit from its provisions.
The convention came into force on January 1, 1988. Twenty-eight states are party to it, including some of our principal trading partners, such as the United States, France, Italy, the Federal Republic of Germany, and China.

The convention constitutes an optional regime that defines the right of the seller and buyer in international
Government Orders
sales of goods between parties whose places of business are in different states, when the states are contracting States, or when the rules of private international law governing the transaction lead to the application of the law of a contracting state.

The convention applies to contracts of sale between parties having their place of business in different states where at least one is party to the convention. It does not apply to contracts for the sale of goods for personal use or such items as electricity, ships, and securities.
The convention applies automatically to contracts subject to it, but as the parties retain the right to make an express derogation, their will always prevails.
The convention establishes rules for the formation of contracts, including rules governing the conclusion of contracts, the periods of time available to offers and the acceptance of offers, as well as formal requirements.
By providing a uniform set of legal rules, the convention addresses a need that has become more acute with the increasing volume of international transactions in goods. It provides greater certainty as to which law governs the contract, facilitates trade between parties in different states and promotes as equitable a relationship as possible between the parties.

As the law of contracts is largely a matter of provincial or territorial jurisdiction, eight provinces and one territory have already passed legislation to implement the convention. They are Ontario, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Manitoba, Newfoundland, Alberta, British Columbia and the Northwest Territories.
The convention includes a clause allowing federal states to accede even if all its territorial units have not passed implementing legislation. The federal implementing legislation will allow all federal entities, even those located in provinces that have not implemented the convention, to benefit from its provisions. Moreover, it will ensure that federal entities are governed by a uniform regime for the international sale of goods.

December 7, 1990

The convention provides for four reservations or declarations.
Article 92 allows a state to declare that it will not be bound by the convention provisions relating to the formation of the contract or by the material provisions relating to contracts for the sale of goods, for example the obligations of the seller and buyer and the passing of risk.
Article 94 allows two or more contracting states with similar legal rules to declare that the convention will not apply between them.
Article 95 allows a state to declare that the convention will not apply to transactions between parties within its territory and parties within the territory of a non-contracting state, even where the rules of private international law lead to the application of the law of the contracting state.
Finally, article 96 allows a state to declare that the provision allowing contracts to be made in any form other than in writing does not apply to transactions involving a party having its place of business within its territory. Following consultations with the provinces and several experts, the Government of Canada has decided not to make any reservations or declarations so that the convention can be given its fullest application.
The Federal Court and all higher courts are courts of competent jurisdiction for the enforcement of the International Sale of Goods Contracts Convention Act. The convention offers several benefits.
First, it standardizes the rules governing the international sale of goods by establishing an international system. However, it does not restrict the freedom of contract because it allows the parties to exempt any contract from the rules of the convention through an expressed derogation clause.
Second, as the convention applies automatically, it can facilitate trade by resolving the issue of which law governs the transaction. This provision is particularly advantageous in goods transactions with states whose commercial law is unfamiliar or even unfavourable to us.
Finally, the convention can reduce the effects of any inequality between trading partners because the weaker partner can ensure application of the convention more easily than the law of its state.
The business community has expressed support for Canada's accession to the convention precisely because of these benefits. In the opinion of experts in civil law and common law the convention is compatible with Canadian law.

Mr. Speaker, in short, passage of the bill implementing the Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods will enable federal departments, departmental corporations and agent Crown corporations, at their option, to benefit from the provisions of the convention in transactions involving the international sale of goods. The convention will likely be applicable for a substantial number of contracts as it is in force for most of our main trading partners.

Canada and other countries first played a role in addressing this problem in 1930 with the International Institute for the Unification of Private Law. They began at that point to try to get a harmonization of trade rules and their efforts brought forward some results. They were interrupted of course by World War II. They continued their efforts until the early 1960s when they came out with some results.
Unfortunately the differences in the legal systems of countries, particularly the differences between the capitalist countries of the western world and the socialist countries in the eastern bloc, did not allow these rules to work. There were too many differences to allow the system that was instituted to be brought into effect.
We went back and through the United Nations, the agency which we have come to depend on more and more in recent years, pushed to develop what we have in Bill C-81. As the minister stated, this is a good bill. It is in the interest of Canada. It is in harmony with Canadian laws. We can support this bill without any difficulty whatsoever.
I think the reason we are number 29 in ratifying this bill probably has little to do with our not moving quickly on it. That might have been the case but I really do not

have any evidence to indicate that. It may be a result of the fact that Canada is a federal country and we had to have the ratification of the provinces. This bill not only deals with trade and commerce, a federal role under the Constitution Act, 1867, but because it also deals with sales it comes under section 92(13) of the property and civil rights provisions of the Constitution. As a result, we had to have the ratification of the provinces.
As the minister has stated, we now have eight provinces which have agreed to it and one territory. It is my understanding that the remaining provinces, Saskatchewan and Quebec, and the remaining territory, the Yukon, have all agreed to ratify it. I commend the minister and the department for bringing this all together. In a federal country it is not always easy to bring things together and to have a consensus.
I would like to reiterate as well that while this is a bill that may not receive a lot of attention, it is very important.
We, as a country, have come to depend very heavily on their national trade. We are also a country that has come to depend very heavily on our trading partners. We have been a country that has helped a lot of countries that have not been as economically successful as we have been.
This is going to be very important to these countries, because it is going to be able to give them a common denominator.
There are ways of accepting countries negotiating a contract under the provisions of this act, either in whole or in part, through the agreement of the countries, but it does provide unless the parties agree otherwise a common denominator that has not only international law behind it, but an international reputation.
To say that this is going to provide all the answers on international trade would be simplistic and misleading. We still have to give interpretation to this convention in the respective courts of the various countries. That is going to provide some difficulties, but I do feel that this has come a long way in helping international trade.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to complete my remarks, and I will take only a few minutes of the time that you have allocated to me.
The roots of the Third World debt crisis lie in a development approach that increases the relationship between the local economies and that of the world and the World Bank system. That is why we have a great concern about continued support, or at least the kind of support as long as the World Bank and the IMF are on the track that they have followed in the last years.
The debt crisis currently is being exacerbated by the requirements of the World Bank and the IMF to adjust measures in order to gain further access for their lending.
By putting on Third World countries or debtor countries, conditions which are detrimental to their economies, the financial institutions have increased the possibility, or the likelihood, that the structure will continue to fail as it has for the last five to ten years.
There is enough evidence out there for this government to take some action, to lead the world in a direction which would make the value of IMF and World Bank funds greater and contribute to the fulfilment of the humanitarian dreams in some cases, humanitarian hopes of debtor countries of the world.
There is evidence to suggest that the IMF's confidence in the structural adjustment process is not too great. There is hope that some place along the way, these institutions will take a good hard look at their method of recalling or eliminating the structural adjustments that they have put in place.

In 1944 and at various times since, the IMF and the World Bank have come together to provide assistance to the Third World. They have become those countries' worst enemies; the worst enemy of real human progress in those countries, because loans that were intended to help are now unmanageable and are causing more disaster than they are help.
I am greatly concerned that we are caught in a systemic malfunction of the world's financial structure and that no one has the guts to admit it, let alone the guts to try and fix it.
We need to take a good look at the structure of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund. We recognize that they have failed in their mandate. These institutions have known this for as long as 12 and 15 years, when I spent some time in Third World countries and worked with the World Bank.
At that time they were recognizing the failures of their policies. Here we are 15 years later, and in the last five years there has been a recognition of the tremendous failure of these two institutions.
In the last five years they have done more harm than good; some good, I recognize, but much harm. They have perpetuated themselves mainly by becoming sacred cows, whose structure and decisions are not questioned by the member countries. The structure and decisions are omnipotent in the eyes of the donor countries. They have convinced the donor countries that if these debts are not paid in full and on time, the world financial structure will collapse. They have forced us as Canadians to choose between the fluidity of the financial institutions and our humanitarian values, the values which we in Canada have tried to make the major values of our community.
This institution, which we are helping to fund, is forcing us as Canadians to choose between the fluidity of that institution and our humanitarian values.
We have to question whether we should go on supporting the World Bank and the IMF, because as they provide assistance to the Third World they have, as I said before, become its worst enemy, and the enemy of real human progress. The loans that were intended to help are now unmanageable. The systemic malfunction of the financial institution is coming back to roost and we do not have the courage to fix it.
